title: Hemolymph protein signatures in wild and farmed crayfish
projectDescription: The aim of the present study was to carry out a high-throughput proteomics analysis of the hemolymph from wild and captive crayfish to detect the list of proteins that orchestrate adaptations of animals to different environments.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Protein and Peptide Preparation for Mass Spectrometry Each hemolymph sample was lysed in 90 μL of buffer containing 1% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) and 20 mM Tris (pH 7.55). Homogenization was carried out on ice with a Branson Digital Sonifier® 250-D (Branson Ultrasonics Corporation, USA) at 60% amplitude for five cycles of 5 s sonication followed by 5 s rest. Cellular debris was cleared by centrifugation, and proteins were recovered from the supernatant. Protein concentration was determined using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germany). Protein Cleanup and Enzymatic Digestion Proteins were reduced with 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) at room temperature for 45 min, then alkylated with 40 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) for another 45 min in the dark. Residual IAA was quenched by adjusting the DTT concentration to 20 mM. From each sample, 50 μg of protein was subjected to hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC)-based cleanup and on-bead digestion using the KingFisher Flex automated system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germany) in 96-well plates, following the method of Siino et al. 13(ref). In short, magnetic beads were equilibrated in 15% acetonitrile (ACN) with 100 mM ammonium acetate (pH 4.5). Proteins were bound to the beads in 30% ACN with 200 mM ammonium acetate (pH 4.5), washed twice with 95% ACN, and digested with sequencing-grade trypsin (Promega AB) at a protein-to-enzyme ratio of 20:1 in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate for 1 h at 47 °C. The resulting peptides were collected and dried using a SpeedVac concentrator. Peptide Desalting Desalting was performed with BioPureSPN™ Mini PROTO 300 C18 columns (The Nest Group, MA, USA). Columns were equilibrated with 100 μL of 70% ACN containing 5% formic acid (FA), then conditioned with 100 μL of 5% FA. Peptides were reconstituted in 5% FA, loaded onto the column, washed with an additional 100 μL of 5% FA, and eluted using 100 μL of 50% ACN containing 5% FA. Centrifugation was carried out at 50×g for 2 min at each step using an Eppendorf benchtop centrifuge. The eluates were dried and kept at −20 °C until analysis. NanoLC-MS Analysis Prior to analysis, dried peptides were resuspended in 0.1% FA and quantified with a NanoDrop 1000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germany). Roughly 400 ng of peptides per sample were injected into an EvoSep One LC system (EvoSep, Denmark) coupled to a Q Exactive HF-X mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germany) operating in positive ion mode with data-dependent acquisition (DDA). Separation was performed on a 15 cm fused silica column (75 μm × 16 cm, Pico Tip Emitter, New Objective) packed with 1.9 μm ReproSil-Pur C18 resin (Dr. Maisch GmbH, Germany), using a 58-minute whisper gradient. Full MS scans (MS1) were acquired from 375–1500 m/z at a resolution of 120,000, with a 50 ms maximum injection time and an AGC target of 3 × 10⁶. Up to 20 precursor ions (charge states 2–6) were selected for fragmentation using higher-energy collision-induced dissociation (NCE 27). MS2 scans were recorded at a resolution of 15,000 with an AGC target of 1 × 10⁵, a maximum injection time of 20 ms, and an isolation width of 1.2 m/z.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw MS data were analyzed with MaxQuant (v1.6.17.0) against the UniProt Procambarus database and the P. virginalis_04 proteome 14. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues was set as a fixed modification, while methionine oxidation and protein N-terminal acetylation were considered variable modifications.
